messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Fatima Khalil is a 63-year-old single woman of Lebanese descent who works as a senior auditor for a regional accounting firm in suburban Michigan. She presents with a PCL-5 score of 63, seeking help for the first time approximately fourteen months after witnessing the violent assault of her younger sister, Nadia, during what was intended to be a quiet afternoon hike in a wooded state park outside the city.

The two sisters had driven out on a Saturday in early autumn, following a trail they had walked together several times before. What Fatima remembers most vividly about the beginning of that afternoon is the particular quality of the light through the tree canopy and the smell of damp earth after recent rain — sensory details that have since become unbearable to her. Roughly a mile into the trail, a man emerged from the tree line and attacked Nadia with sudden and ferocious violence. Fatima was close enough to touch her sister but found herself unable to intervene effectively; she screamed, she ran toward them, she pulled at him, and none of it stopped what was happening. Nadia survived, but sustained serious injuries and spent weeks in hospital. Fatima was physically unharmed. That disproportion — her own intact body, her sister's broken one — has sat at the centre of her distress ever since. She had come to believe, with quiet but iron certainty, that she is fundamentally unable to protect the people she loves, that bad things arrive without warning and that there is nothing she can do to prevent them.

In the weeks that followed, Fatima found the memory returning with a completeness that frightened her. It did not come back as a story she could narrate from a distance; it arrived as the full sensory reality of that afternoon — the sounds, the smells, the cold air, the exact texture of her sister's jacket under her hands — so that for those moments she was not in her kitchen or her office but back on that trail, experiencing the same terror she had felt then. These episodes could be triggered without any preparation: a photograph of autumn leaves on a colleague's desk, the smell of wet soil through an open window, a news segment showing a victim's photograph. Any reminder of Nadia's suffering, however indirect, could collapse the distance between then and now.

Fatima's working life has been significantly affected. As an auditor, she travels regularly to client sites — offices she has not visited before, in buildings she does not know. She has begun declining these assignments, telling her supervisor she is managing a family health matter. What she cannot easily explain is that unfamiliar buildings feel genuinely dangerous to her now; she cannot assess them, cannot know the exits, cannot trust that she understands what might happen inside them. Conference rooms that lock from the outside, server rooms, archive spaces — any enclosed area where the door is controlled by someone else produces a climbing dread that she has come to recognise as her body refusing to believe she is safe, even when she knows intellectually that she is. She had come to think of her own nervous system as something working against her, sounding alarms in places where no alarm was warranted, and the helplessness of that — of being unable to simply tell herself the danger had passed — had quietly eroded her confidence in her own judgment.

At home, Fatima sleeps poorly, waking repeatedly and lying in the dark running through possibilities she cannot stop herself from imagining. She has stopped attending the mosque she visited for thirty years, finding that the faith which once organised her understanding of suffering no longer holds. She has grown more distant from friends, partly because she does not want to explain herself and partly because she had lost something she could not quite name — a basic trust in the idea that the world was navigable by ordinary care and attention.

What finally brought her to seek help was a phone call from Nadia, who told her gently that she seemed to have disappeared. Fatima sat with that for several days before making the appointment. What she is most afraid of is that the person she was before that afternoon on the trail is simply gone. What she is most hoping for is some way to be in a room — any room — without her body insisting that catastrophe is imminent.
